In the Delhi region of India, the native language was Khariboli, whose earliest form is called Old Hindi (or Hindavi).
In cities such as Delhi, the ancient language Old Hindi began to acquire many Persian loanwords and continued to be called "Hindi" and later, also "Hindustani".

By the end of the reign of Aurangzeb in the early 1700s, the common language around Delhi began to be called Zaban-e-Urdu, a name derived from the Turkic word ordu (army) or orda and is said to have arisen as the "language of the camp", or "Zaban-i-Ordu" means "Language of High camps" or natively "Lashkari Zaban" means "Language of Army" even though the term Urdu held different meanings at that time.
